title: AI adoption is broadening faster than trust, capability and sovereignty arrangements can stabilize
geography: 15-country public-attitudes survey spanning advanced and emerging economies, with global AI-economy modeling and country comparisons

observations.period: 2026; Public First AI Global survey and economic model

importance.value: on average, 45% say AI will change the world significantly and 46% say it already has; 64% say AI is the most important current technology and their country should be a leader

opportunity_condition.value: the report's model estimates that around 47% of potential economic opportunity over the next five years depends on choices about adoption, workflow integration and preparedness

adoption_boundary.value: the report estimates that only around 8% of the wider potential economic dividend has been realized so far

observations.method: Public First polling across 15 countries combined with a global economic model covering task verification, workflow integration, innovation and distributional effects.
observations.uncertainty: The economic percentages are model outputs dependent on assumptions about adoption, task substitution, verification and workflow redesign; they are not observed GDP, productivity or welfare effects.
observations.subgroup: Adults in advanced and emerging economies, workers exposed to different task structures, firms deciding how to integrate AI, and countries competing for AI capability.
observations.counterinterpretation: High perceived importance does not guarantee useful adoption, and modeled opportunity can overstate gains if verification, organizational change, energy, labor or governance constraints are harder than assumed.

observations.period: 2023-2026; repeated Public First attitudes waves and 2026 country comparisons

denominator.unit: countries included in the 2026 public-attitudes survey

western_backlash.value: net positive sentiment toward AI fell sharply in the United States and United Kingdom over the repeated waves; the report describes the decline as around 75%

geographic_divergence.value: sentiment remains more positive in several Asian and emerging economies, while younger and older groups in advanced economies are less positive than middle-aged groups

shallow_diffusion.value: regular use is broadening, but users report applying AI to only around a quarter of daily tasks and 56% of advanced-economy users say they began within the past year

observations.method: Repeated and cross-country survey comparisons of emotional valence, regular use, age patterns and self-reported task coverage.
observations.uncertainty: Net valence depends on question wording and coding of positive and negative emotions; self-reported task coverage does not measure quality, duration, productivity or whether AI is embedded invisibly in software.
observations.subgroup: US and UK adults, Asian and emerging-market respondents, younger users, older users, regular users and people newly adopting AI.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower sentiment may reflect greater awareness and scrutiny rather than rejection, while positive sentiment in high-adoption markets may reflect optimism, necessity, social desirability or different expectations.

observations.period: 2026; reported AI use and sophistication in advanced economies

denominator.unit: advanced-economy AI-user comparison in the Public First survey

sophistication_gap.value: higher-income users are 2.1 times more likely to be sophisticated users than users with only secondary education; university-educated users are 1.5 times more likely; users under 35 are 2.5 times more likely than users over 50

firm_gap.value: workers at larger enterprises are around 1.1 times more likely to be sophisticated users than workers at small and medium-sized businesses

agent_privacy.value: only 29% say they would be comfortable giving an AI agent access to their bank account, while comfort is higher for some health-data and calendar uses

observations.method: Survey comparison of self-described AI use sophistication, demographic and firm-size characteristics, workforce enablement and willingness to share sensitive data with agents.
observations.uncertainty: The associations do not establish whether income, education, age, firm size, support or prior experience causes sophisticated use; the report's categories are constructed from survey responses.
observations.subgroup: Higher- and lower-income users, users with different education levels and ages, SMB and large-enterprise workers, and people considering agent access to financial or health data.
observations.counterinterpretation: A sophistication gap may reflect access to better tools, time, training and organizational permission rather than individual capability; privacy reluctance may be a rational safeguard rather than a barrier to beneficial use.

observations.period: 2026; AI sovereignty, infrastructure and relational use debates

denominator.unit: countries included in the Public First survey

sovereignty.value: 77% say it is important to keep data within their country; 19% of non-American respondents say they do not trust an American AI model, even though many continue to use major US-origin tools

infrastructure_politics.value: the United States is described as unusually divided or negative about building more data centres, with concerns including electricity bills, taxpayer costs and environmental damage

relational_ai.value: one in five respondents say they have used AI for emotional advice and one in six say they have a relationship with an AI

observations.method: Cross-country survey questions on model origin, data location, data-centre expansion, emotional advice and relationships with AI.
observations.uncertainty: Trust, relationship and sovereignty responses are culturally and politically contingent; the report does not define relationship intensity, verify behavior or measure infrastructure impacts directly.
observations.subgroup: Respondents in countries with different AI ecosystems and geopolitical alignments, local communities near data-centre development, users seeking emotional support and people concerned about national data control.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stated support for data sovereignty can coexist with practical dependence on foreign platforms; reported AI relationships may range from casual anthropomorphism to sustained emotional reliance.

related_sources.claim: Public First AI Global opportunity chapter covering task structure, verification, workflow integration and modeled economic potential.
Public First AI Global attitudes chapter covering sentiment, usage depth, sophistication and agent-data comfort.
Public First AI Global debates chapter covering jobs, model sovereignty, data centres and AI relationships.

boundary: This record adds an AI public-attitudes, sovereignty, infrastructure and capability layer linking adoption to sentiment, task design, training and support, sensitive-data trust, model origin, data-centre politics and relational use. It combines a 15-country survey with economic modeling; it is not respondent-level ingestion, a causal evaluation, verified behavioral telemetry, a complete global public-opinion census or proof of realized economic effects.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Public First AI Global 2026 publication was reviewed for the 18,000-plus respondent and 15-country frame, modeled opportunity claims, sentiment change, shallow and sophisticated use, agent-data comfort, model-origin trust, data sovereignty, data-centre views and relational AI claims.
